title: Shloka 91
subtitle: Seated on the principles, hidden in the sheaths, flushed with wine

namas.translation: The ranked principles out of which the world is built serve her as a seat.

compound.gloss: she whose seat is the constituent principles

children.gloss: a true principle, a constituent reality

namas.translation: She is the 'that' of the great Upaniṣadic sentence, the reality a word can point at but never hold.

morphology.note: the word tattvamayī is read by commentators as the three names tat, tvam and ayī

namas.translation: She is the 'thou' of that same sentence, the self addressed in the second person and found to be nothing other than the first.

morphology.note: the second-person pronoun is not marked for gender

namas.translation: Taken as the particle of address, this name is the calling out itself, the bare act of turning toward her.

morphology.note: an indeclinable of address, lengthened to ayī where the verse divides tattvamayī

namas.translation: She stands inside the five wrappings of the self, further in than any of them reaches.

compound.gloss: she who abides within the five sheaths

namas.translation: Her greatness overruns every boundary anyone might try to set around it.

morphology.note: a bahuvrīhi closing in the an-stem mahiman keeps that stem in the feminine

compound.gloss: she whose majesty has no limit

namas.translation: Her youth does not pass into anything else; she stands permanently at its height.
A wine-like exhilaration fills her and shows itself in every movement.

compound.gloss: she who is richly furnished with rapture

children.gloss: she who abounds in, is amply provided with

commentary.meaning: Eight names, and they fall into two halves that could almost belong to different hymns. The first line is technical. She is seated on the tattvas; she is the great Upaniṣadic sentence taken apart into its words; she stands inside the five sheaths. This is the vocabulary of the philosophical schools, and it places her at the far end of an analysis — the principle on which the world's constituents rest, the referent of both "that" and "thou", the thing found when the wrappings of a human being are removed one at a time. The second line does not continue the analysis. It says that her greatness has no border, that her youth never turns into anything else, and that she is filled with a wine-like exhilaration. The turn is the point of the verse. Having driven the description as far inward as the categories can take it, the hymn arrives not at a bare absolute but at someone flushed, unaging and laughing — and the four names of the verse that follows will do nothing but describe what that intoxication looks like on her face.
commentary.history:
Tattva is one of the plainest words in philosophical Sanskrit and one of the hardest to translate. It is the pronoun tad, "that", with the abstract suffix -tva: that-ness, the state of being what a thing is. So a tattva is a reality in the strict sense, a principle that is not reducible to anything further down the list, and each school of Indian philosophy is partly identifiable by how many it counts. Sāṃkhya counts twenty-five, running from the five gross elements up through the senses, mind, ego and intellect to unmanifest nature and, standing apart from all of it, the conscious witness. The Śaiva and Śākta systems accept that list and extend it upward by eleven more, adding the veils that individuate consciousness — the constraints of time, limited agency, limited knowledge, desire and fate, together with māyā — and above those the pure principles that end in Śiva and Śakti. Either way, a tattva is a rung, and the whole set is the ladder by which the world is built downward from consciousness into matter.

Tattvāsanā is a bahuvrīhi: she whose seat is the tattvas. What the compound does with that ladder is startling if you have just been reading Sāṃkhya. The entire apparatus of world-construction, the thirty-six principles that between them account for everything there is, is here demoted to furniture. She sits on it. The hymn is fond of this move and makes it more than once, seating her elsewhere on a couch whose supports are the five great gods; the point in every case is that whatever a system takes as its ultimate terms turns out, in her case, to be the thing beneath her.

The second word of the verse is written as a single unit, tattvamayī, "made of the tattvas", and the received list of a thousand names divides it into three: tat, tvam, ayī. This is one of a handful of places where the count only comes out right if a written word is broken, and the commentators generally accept the division rather than argue for it. What it yields is the great sentence of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, tat tvam asi, "that thou art", which Uddālaka Āruṇi repeats nine times to his son Śvetaketu — with one substitution. The copula asi, "thou art", has been replaced by ayi, the ordinary Sanskrit particle of address, lengthened here to fit. The statement of identity has become a calling out. Read as one word, the name says she is the substance of everything; read as three, it says she is the subject of that identity and also the vocative in which someone turns toward her. Both readings stand in the tradition, and neither cancels the other.

Kośa means a sheath, the scabbard a sword goes into, and also a treasury and a bud. The five sheaths belong to the second chapter of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, which proceeds by a repeated formula: within this one, another, further in. The self made of food gives way to one made of breath, that to one made of mind, that to one made of understanding, and that to one made of bliss. Each is described as having the shape of a bird, with a head, wings and a tail, and each is said to be filled by the next. Later Vedānta made this into a standard method of self-inquiry, peeling the layers to find what is not any of them. Pañcakośāntarasthitā places her at the end of that peeling. She is not a sixth sheath; she is what abiding within all five means.

The last three names let the pressure out. Niḥsīma-mahimā uses mahiman, the abstract noun of greatness — the same word that stands behind the ritual phrase for a god's own majesty — and denies it any sīman, any boundary line of the sort that separates one field from the next. Nityayauvanā fixes her at the age the tradition always visualizes her at, sixteen, an age that in this school is also a number of syllables and a name of the goddess. And mada, the last word, is the word for wine, for the intoxication wine produces, and for the rut-fluid that runs down a bull elephant's temples in season. The commentators generally read it in two registers at once: as the ritual wine of the left-hand offering, and as the bliss of her union with Śiva, described in yogic terms as a nectar flowing at the crown of the head. The hymn does not choose between them, and it does not apologise for the word.
commentary.practice:
The first line is a run of dental stops and it will punish carelessness. Tattvāsanā opens with tat, closed firmly on the teeth, and then tvā — so the doubled t is genuinely doubled, held for a beat, with the v released after it as its own consonant and the ā long. Say tat-tvā-sa-nā rather than letting the cluster collapse into something like "tatwa". The same cluster returns immediately in tattvamayī, which is the whole difficulty of the line: two nearly identical four-syllable words in a row, differing only in their endings.

When this verse is used for archanā, name by name with an offering at each, it produces one of the few real irregularities in the whole stotra. Almost every name in the hymn is a feminine ā-stem and takes the dative ending -āyai, and the ear comes to expect it. Here the ear is broken three times over. Tat becomes tasmai, the neuter dative of the demonstrative; tvam becomes tubhyam, the dative of the second-person pronoun; ayī becomes ayyai. And niḥsīmamahimā, because it ends in the an-stem mahiman rather than in -ā, takes niḥsīmamahimne, which looks and sounds masculine and is simply what that declension does. Reciters who have learned the -āyai ending as a reflex regularly stumble at these four, and the remedy is to learn them as exceptions before the reflex sets in rather than after.

Pañcakośāntarasthitā is eight syllables and fills the second half of the line by itself. It hides a join: kośa ends in short a, antar begins in short a, and the two combine into the long ā of kośāntara. Knowing that keeps the vowel long, which the metre requires. The cluster sth in sthitā is a dental s followed by an aspirated dental th, with no vowel between them and no English "th" sound anywhere in the vicinity — release the s directly into a t with breath behind it.

In the second line, niḥsīma begins with a visarga, normally heard as a light breath carrying a faint echo of the preceding vowel before the s; do not turn it into a full syllable. Nityayauvanā contains au, which is a full-length diphthong and takes twice the time of a short vowel; clipping it toward the vowel of English "cow" is the commonest fault in the line. Madaśālinī ends in a long ī and gives madaśālinyai in the dative, where the ī contracts to y before the ending.

The caesura falls where the anuṣṭubh always puts it, after the sixteenth syllable, which here is the end of pañcakośāntarasthitā. That is the seam between the philosophical half of the verse and the intoxicated half, and it is the only place to breathe.

As for what the verse asks of the person chanting it: the second line is not decoration attached to the first. A reciter trained in Vedānta will want to hurry past mada, or to convert it into a metaphor before it has been allowed to mean anything. The verse puts the analysis and the wine in the same breath group on purpose. What is found inside the five sheaths, it says, is not an abstraction but something with a face, and the face is flushed.

crossReferences.iast: sa ya eṣo 'ṇimaitadātmyam idaṃ sarvaṃ tat satyaṃ sa ātmā tat tvam asi śvetaketo iti |
crossReferences.translation: That which is this fineness — all this has that for its self. That is the real. That is the self. That thou art, Śvetaketu.
crossReferences.relevance: The sentence the three names tat, tvam and ayī are cut out of. Uddālaka repeats it nine times to his son at the end of a long argument, each time after a different illustration, and the repetition is what fixed it in the tradition as one of the great statements of identity. The hymn keeps the two pronouns and drops the verb, putting a cry of address where the assertion of being was.

crossReferences.source: Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2 (the formula of the sheaths)
crossReferences.iast: tasmād vā etasmād annarasamayād anyo 'ntara ātmā prāṇamayaḥ |
crossReferences.translation: Other than and within this one made of the essence of food is a self made of breath.
crossReferences.relevance: The sentence pattern that generates the five sheaths, repeated with a new pair of terms at each stage until it reaches the self made of bliss. The word antara, "within", is the same word that stands at the centre of pañcakośāntarasthitā, and the Upaniṣad's insistent movement inward is exactly what the name compresses into a single compound.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Theosophical Publishing House, Adyar; repeatedly reprinted since 1899)
references.note: The only complete English rendering of the eighteenth-century commentary that later tradition treats as authoritative, and the place to see how a commentator justifies dividing a written word like tattvamayī into three separate names. The translation is Victorian and stiff, and Sastry sometimes paraphrases where Bhāskararāya argues, but nothing else in English does the job.

references.title: Upaniṣads
references.author: tr. Patrick Olivelle (Oxford World's Classics, 1996)
references.note: Read Chāndogya 6 whole rather than the one sentence everyone quotes: the nine illustrations Uddālaka builds toward tat tvam asi are what give the phrase its force. Olivelle's Taittirīya 2 is also the clearest English on the five sheaths, and his notes are honest about where the Sanskrit is obscure.

references.title: Classical Sāṃkhya: An Interpretation of Its History and Meaning
references.author: Gerald James Larson (Motilal Banarsidass, 2nd ed. 1979)
references.note: Worth an afternoon if the word tattva has so far been a piece of atmosphere rather than a technical term. Larson lays out the twenty-five principles and what work each one does, which is the necessary background to seeing what tattvāsanā claims by putting her on top of the whole set.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Sir Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899; searchable at the Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries)
references.note: Look up mada here before deciding what it means in this verse. The entry runs from the rut-fluid of elephants through wine, sexual desire, pride and ecstasy without separating them, which is a fair picture of how the word behaves in the four names that follow.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The standard scholarly introduction to Śrīvidyā, and the best short account of how this tradition holds together Vedāntic language about the self and frankly tantric language about wine and the body. Useful precisely at the seam this verse sits on.
